module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Written on the Wall II - Conjecture 59

*References:*
- [E. DeLaVina, Written on the Wall II, Conjectures of Graffiti.pc](http://cms.dt.uh.edu/faculty/delavinae/research/wowII/)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace WrittenOnTheWallII.GraphConjecture59

open SimpleGraph

variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nontrivial α]

/--
WOWII [Conjecture 59](http://cms.dt.uh.edu/faculty/delavinae/research/wowII/)

For a simple connected graph $G$, the size $f(G)$ of a largest induced forest
satisfies $f(G) \ge \lceil \sqrt{\mathrm{residue}(G) \cdot b(G)} \rceil$, where
$\mathrm{residue}(G)$ is the Havel-Hakimi residue (the number of zeros remaining
after applying the Havel-Hakimi algorithm to the degree sequence until termination)
and $b(G)$ is the size of a largest induced bipartite subgraph.

See: Favaron, Mahéo, Saclé (1991) for the residue; DeLaVina's Graffiti.pc for the conjecture.

This conjecture is false. There is a connected counterexample on 123 vertices
with `residue G = 101`, `b G = 122`, and `G.largestInducedForestSize = 111`.
Indeed, `101 * 122 = 12322 = 111 ^ 2 + 1`, so the conjectured lower bound is 112.

There is also an 18-vertex counterexample. Take a bipartite chain graph on
vertices `0, ..., 9`, with parts `{0, ..., 4}` and `{5, ..., 9}`, a hub `10`
adjacent to every core vertex, and leaves `11, ..., 17` attached at the hub.
It has residue 10, `b = 17`, and largest induced forest 13.
`⌈√170⌉ = 14`, so it falsifies the bound.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5,
  formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/QDKStorm/wowii59-counterexample/blob/main/Counterexample59.lean",
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at "https://github.com/anagnorisis2peripeteia/formal-conjectures/blob/69388817d384ea44a5ef4b2aed1097c8281f9c3a/FormalConjectures/WrittenOnTheWallII/GraphConjecture59.lean"]
theorem conjecture59 : answer(False) ↔
    ∀ (α : Type) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nontrivial α]
      (G : SimpleGraph α) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (_ : G.Connected),
      ⌈Real.sqrt ((residue G : ℝ) * b G)⌉ ≤ (G.largestInducedForestSize : ℝ) := by
  sorry

-- Sanity checks

/-- The `largestInducedForestSize` is nonneg. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
example (G : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) : 0 ≤ G.largestInducedForestSize := Nat.zero_le _

/-- The residue of $K_2$ equals $1$: degree sequence is $[1, 1]$; one Havel-Hakimi
step gives $[0]$, leaving a single zero. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
example : residue (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)) = 1 := by
  simp [residue, Fin.univ_succ, Multiset.sort_cons, residueAux, havelHakimiStep]

end WrittenOnTheWallII.GraphConjecture59

findings.description: The docstring's 18-vertex counterexample does not say which chain graph to use: "Take a bipartite chain graph on vertices 0..9, with parts {0..4} and {5..9}, a hub 10 adjacent to every core vertex, and leaves 11..17 attached at the hub. It has residue 10, b = 17, and largest induced forest 13." The stated invariants hold only for particular chain graphs. I brute-forced this construction with the repository's own `residueAux` and exhaustive subset checks for f and b. Model the core as x_i ~ y_j iff j < d_i, with d_0 ≥ … ≥ d_4. Only 6 of the 252 such cores give a counterexample; e.g. d = (5,5,4,3,2) gives (res,b,f) = (10,17,13). Two standard chain graphs do not work. With core K_{5,5} the graph has (res,b,f) = (9,17,13), and ⌈√153⌉ = 13 ≤ 13. With core the half graph H_5, d = (5,4,3,2,1), it has (11,17,14), and ⌈√187⌉ = 14 ≤ 14. So the remark cannot be checked as written, and read literally it is false for most chain graphs. The formal statement is not affected.
findings.source_evidence: The WOWII source does not mention this construction; it lists #59 as "O" (open). The evidence is computational: Lean #eval runs with the repository's `SimpleGraph.residueAux` plus brute-force f/b on the 18-vertex graphs. d=[5,5,4,3,2] → (10, f 13, b 17); d=[5,5,5,5,5] → (9, 13, 17); d=[5,4,3,2,1] → (11, 14, 17).
findings.suggested_fix: Name the chain graph explicitly. For example: "vertex i ∈ {0,…,4} is adjacent to 5,…,4+d_i with (d_0,…,d_4) = (5,5,4,3,2)", or give its edge list. Otherwise, drop the 18-vertex remark and point to the formal proof.

status_issues.source_status: The linked Lean file is only a partial certificate. It proves the vertex count 123, connectivity, the sorted degree sequence, residueAux = 101 / residue = 101 (by native_decide), ⌈√(101·122)⌉ = 112, and ¬(⌈√(101·122)⌉ ≤ 111). It never formalizes b(G) = 122 or f(G) = 111, nor even the needed bounds b ≥ 122 and f ≤ 111, and it never states the disproof. The repository has a single commit, so the file was never a complete proof. The link also points to `main`, which is not a stable reference.
status_issues.evidence: QDKStorm README: "It checks the explicit graph's cardinality, connectedness, sorted degree sequence, graph-level residue, ceiling value, and numerical violation. The exact values of `b(G)` and `f(G)` are established by the proof above and by the structural certificate verifier; they are not yet fully formalized in Lean." (https://github.com/QDKStorm/wowii59-counterexample). PROOFS.md requires that the linked statement imply the repository statement and that the link be stable.
status_issues.suggested_change: Remove the `formal_proof using lean4` attribute, or replace it with a commit-pinned link to a complete formal proof. The QDKStorm repository can be cited in the docstring as the source of the informal (partly machine-checked) 123-vertex counterexample. Keep `research solved` and `answer(False)`: the disproof is correct.

reformulations.difference: The source states a conjecture: every simple connected graph satisfies f(G) ≥ CEIL[sqrt[res(G)*b(G)]]. The Lean differs in form in four ways. (1) It is written `answer(False) ↔ ∀ …`, i.e. ¬∀, recording the disproof. (2) It adds `[Nontrivial α]`, which excludes the one-vertex graph. (3) Vertex types range over `Type` only. (4) The integer ceiling is cast to ℝ and compared with the cast forest number.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (1) `answer(False)` elaborates to `False`, and `False ↔ P` is ¬P. That matches the source's claim being false; sibling disproved WOWII files (e.g. 23, 32, 33, 58) use the same pattern. (2) The only connected graph excluded by `Nontrivial` is K1, where res = b = f = 1 and ⌈√1⌉ = 1 ≤ 1 holds. So the ∀ with `Nontrivial` is equivalent to the ∀ without it. I proved this ↔ in Lean (`nontrivial_harmless`, axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). (3) Every finite graph is isomorphic to one on `Fin n : Type`, and all the invariants are isomorphism-invariant. (4) For an integer z and natural f, (z:ℝ) ≤ (f:ℝ) iff z ≤ f. The definitions `residue` (Havel–Hakimi, sorted descending), `largestInducedBipartiteSubgraphSize`/`b` and `largestInducedForestSize` (sSup over bounded nonempty sets of Finset cards) match WOWII definitions 42, 15 and 41.

review.notes:
No misformalization in `conjecture59`. The source (WOWII all.html, Wayback snapshot 2026-07-23) says: "59. If G is a simple connected graph, then f(G) ≥ CEIL[sqrt[res(G)*b(G)]]", status "O", dated Mar 25, 2004. The live cms.dt.uh.edu / cms.uhd.edu site was unreachable over HTTPS from the sandbox. No other WOWII entry uses this expression. The related #38, f ≥ CEIL[(res+b)/2], is marked F; since √(rb) ≤ (r+b)/2, #59 is the weaker bound.

On the status: WOWII still marks #59 "O", while the file says `research solved` with `answer(False)`. The file is ahead of the source, not stale. I checked the 123-vertex counterexample (cone over the 7-regular cyclic bipartite graph on 12+12 vertices plus 98 isolated vertices):
- residueAux [122, 8^24, 1^98] = 101 (Lean #eval).
- b = 122: G−u is bipartite, and u,x0,y0 is a triangle.
- f = 111: the edge-count argument gives f(B) = 13, a perfect matching gives α(B) = 12, and the cone argument gives max(98+13, 1+98+12).
- 101·122 = 12322 = 111²+1, so ⌈√⌉ = 112 > 111.

I also brute-forced an 18-vertex instance (chain core with neighbourhood sizes 5,5,4,3,2): res 10, b 17, f 13. So no category or answer change is needed; only the lean4 `formal_proof` record is inaccurate.

Sanity checks:
- `residueAux` gives the standard values on K1, K2, P3, K3, K4, K_{1,3}, C4, C5, K_{3,3}.
- Exhaustive search over all labeled connected graphs on 2–6 vertices (1, 4, 38, 728, 26704 graphs) finds no violation. This fits Graffiti.pc having generated the conjecture from its database, so the definitions do not create spurious small counterexamples.
- The two `example` tests are correct (residue(K2) = 1 matches WOWII's definition).
